title: Web Attack: Selecting Controls
context: A public web application is suffering from SQL injections and customer data exfiltration attempts. You must deploy three relevant controls and justify their limits.

n1.text: Which control blocks SQL injections in HTTP traffic before reaching the application?

choices.text: A WAF placed in front of the web application
choices.why: A WAF inspects the HTTP application layer and blocks injection patterns.

choices.text: A NIDS in detection mode on the segment
choices.why: A NIDS would alert, but would not block the request.
A decoy helps detect, not block an attack on the real application.

n2.text: Attackers are now attempting to exfiltrate customer files from an internal workstation. Which control best targets this risk?

choices.text: DLP on the endpoint agent and at network egress
choices.why: DLP identifies sensitive data and blocks its egress, on the workstation or at the proxy.

choices.text: HIPS on the web server only
choices.why: HIPS protects the host, not outbound data flow from the workstation.
BIMI displays a brand logo: unrelated to exfiltration.

n3.text: To detect an attacker searching for accounts early, which decoy should you deploy?

choices.text: A honeytoken and a canary account that are never used legitimately
choices.why: Any use of these decoys is a high-confidence signal, with no business false positives.

choices.text: A real administrator account with a weak password
choices.why: A real weak account is a vulnerability, not a controlled decoy.
Without logs, you lose the very signal you need.

n4.outcome: You blocked the injection at the application layer, stopped exfiltration with DLP, and detected reconnaissance using decoys.

debrief: WAF protects the application layer; NIDS alerts without blocking.
DLP acts on outbound data; EDR/XDR acts on endpoint behavior.
Decoys (honeytoken, canary) produce high-value signals without false positives.
